extracted.intended_audience: newspaper readers and wire-service editors (general public; journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and formatting Associated Press (wire) news dispatches: concise datelined leads followed by sourced detail, quotes, background and technical/contextual information for publication and syndication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and byline format
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispatches open with a dateline in the form CITY, MONTH DAY-(AP)- (often in all caps) and sometimes include bureau/service qualifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on page: "WASHINGTON, MARCH 17-(AP)-", "SAN FRANCISCO, MARCH 27--(AP)-", and parenthetical markers such as "(AP SPECIAL WASHINGTON SERVICE)". Dateline signals location and date for editors/readers and identifies the AP origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise lead paragraph summarizing main facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The first paragraph (lead) quickly summarizes the essential who/what/where/when/why of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "ENLISTED MEN IN KOREA WHO WANT TO TOTE PERSO 1X-@HOOTERS...ARE GIVING HEADACHES TO THE MILITARY" and "DEVELOPMENT OF THE FIRST FULLY-AUTOMATIC PARACHUTING ESCAPE UNIT...WAS DISCLOSED TODAY BY THE NAVY." Leads are short, direct and set the news frame for the rest of the dispatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and identification of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements, opinions and facts are attributed with the speaker's name and identifying title or affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "SENATOR HENNINGS (D-MO) SAID", "BRIG. GEN. WILLIAM P. NUCKOLS, CHIEF U.N. SPOKESMAN," and named experts or officials are cited when quoted or paraphrased. Titles, party and state (for politicians) or job title (for officials) are included to establish authority and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of direct quotes and paraphrase with context
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported speech appears as direct quotations or paraphrase, and is clearly attributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quoted passages like "WE HAVE A NATIONAL LOYALTY PROGRAM LOADED DOWN WITH AFFRONTS TO CIVIL LIBERTIES," and paraphrases such as "THE REDS PROMISED TO CONSIDER THE MODIFICATION." Quotes are used to present exact language; paraphrase condenses or summarizes positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of technical and contextual detail after the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the lead, stories expand with technical descriptions, test results, background history or operational details to explain significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the ejection-seat story continues with human and dummy tests, speeds tested ("500 miles an hour"), sequence of mechanisms (stabilizing chute, preset cartridge, cable release) and altitude timing. This guidance shows that technical detail and testing context belong in subsequent paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wire-service codes and length markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric parenthetical codes appear throughout (e.g., (280), (350), (450)) likely indicating story length, wire category or internal routing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: standalone numbers in parentheses precede or follow stories and subheads, e.g. "(280) PMS BJT." and "(350)". Editors use these codes for ordering, trimming or processing wire copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service/location tags and special-service labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Parenthetical service labels indicate special reporting or the dispatch source (e.g., AP special services, bureau identifiers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "AP SPECIAL WASHINGTON SERVICE", "FIRST LEAD INFORMATION" and other parenthetical markers that inform editors about origin or special handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/embargo and reuse instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some items include explicit release/use times or notes indicating when copy is cleared for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "FOR USE AT 1 P.M. EASTERN STANDARD TIME TODAY MON.MARCH17" — indicates an embargo or scheduled release time that publishers should respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced reporting / presentation of multiple sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage presents different perspectives, reporting positions, denials or counterclaims from opposing parties rather than taking a single side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in truce/parleys coverage both Allied and Communist positions are quoted and described (e.g., "THE REDS PROMISED..." and allied objections). This demonstrates a norm of including competing viewpoints and official positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, objective tone and economy of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispatches favor factual, economical wording with limited editorializing and use short paragraphs to convey information efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories use straightforward declarative sentences, minimal flourish, and short paragraphs (typical AP style). Headlines and lead lines are punchy and factual rather than opinionated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of headlines, subheads and capitalization conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines and section identifiers frequently use uppercase and brief, attention-getting phrasing to identify stories or beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: all-caps headlines and section markers (e.g., "SIX-SHOOTERS", "BELLY FLYING", "COMMUNIST UNIONS") are used to orient readers and organize multiple dispatches on a page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of human-interest/detail anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories often include small humanizing details or anecdotes to illustrate broader points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the revolver-mailing piece, the anecdote "So when Willie writes home and says 'MA, SEND ME A REVOLVER,' she just wraps it up and takes it to the postoffice." Such details provide color and relatable context in otherwise policy/operations stories.
